newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian retail reversal fuels rate cut talk.
newsitem.headline: Australian retail reversal fuels rate cut talk.

text.p: Australia's retail sector may have celebrated a false dawn earlier this year, judging by data released on Friday which cast doubt on the sustainability of the strength of a rebound seen in first quarter consumption.
The value of Australia's retail trade fell by 1.7 percent in April, in contrast to a median forecast of a 0.5 percent rise in a Reuters survey of 29 economists.
The fall was seen justifying the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) decision to cut official interest rates last week, and set the market talking about the likelihood of another cut in rates.
"It certainly indicates weakness in the economy," Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen. "It certainly throws open the prospect of further rate cuts," he added.
April's fall followed a 0.3 percent fall in March, making it the first time retail trade has fallen in consecutive months since July and August of 1993.

Adding to the concerns about consumption was a 6.0 percent fall in April new motor vehicle registrations, although this was mitigated by the fact that registrations had risen by almost 10 percent in the first three months of 1997.

Private consumption is expected to be a key driver of first quarter gross domestic product (GDP), due out next Wednesday, because after a disappointing Christmas period, retail trade rose 2.2 percent in real terms in the March quarter.
However, the strength was concentrated in January and February and analysts said it may have been a temporary blip due to buying at the post-Chrismas sales, with underlying demand remaining subdued.
In April, department store sales fell 9.5 percent, and are now at their lowest level since last September.
"It's got to now cast some doubts on the sustainability of the bounce in Q1 of private consumption," HSBC Markets economist Anthony Thompson said of the April retail data.

As the strength in consumption, with its flow-through effects to jobs and production, was seen as one of the reasons to be optimistic about the economy's prospects, signs of renewed weakness raised the prospects of further rate cuts.

"It will definitely add to speculation of another cut, because it's a case of if the consumer doesn't come in, employment will never kick in," Citibank Australia senior economist Annette Beacher said.
